Will anything replace HTML and CSS?

Eventually yes, but it will take some major cultural changes in software development to make it happen. HTML, JavaScript and CSS are long in the tooth technologies that have been squeezed for all their juice for too long now. We've been taking these disjointed technologies and trying to tightly integrate them for years but instead of getting a cohesive technology stack we seem to have just created a Frankenstein's monster that won't die. The browser was intended to deliver formatted content. Applications were shoehorned onto the browser when it would have been better to separate applications from content browsing. Java applets and later technologies like Flash, Adobe Flex and MS Silverlight attempted to give the browser a better set of tools to build applications rather than forcing a content rendering platform to fake it. Because these alternative technologies were proprietary they were seen as a dead end to an open web. Open standards then became the chosen path but it always seems like the lack of a central group to plan web technologies and nurture them through their development has left us with a random mix of mediocre technologies that have short lives due to the winners being chosen by short lived popularity. I'm all for FOSS but I've grown weary of never reaching any sustainable momentum in any given project before it forks into 100 different variations that quickly diverge for minor improvements. For all the bad that proprietary software is, it birthed the browser and the associated technologies and we only stand here today because there was a central, albeit profit-oriented, group who funded it into long term existence. Open source projects rarely have staying power and with only major exceptions like GNU Linux we just don't have cohesion (although I would say Linux would have died long ago if Linus Torvalds didn't control the kernel as he does).

Given all this I think we should focus some very concentrated effort on making an open but centrally managed new set of tools and platforms to replace the browser, HTML, CSS and JavaScript. We need something that can allow developers to build rich and powerful applications that fully leverage the Internet's transport technologies while simultaneously granting the end user extremely granular control over security and privacy features so we don't have abuses. This new platform/technology stack should be well planned by an architecture group that listens to the development and user communities while looking towards a long term development path that allows for a mutable, scalable and portable future with strong standards. The browser itself should evolve to be an application that runs on this new platform rather than the other-way-round as we have it now. This would allow for a tight and seamless integration of applications into operating systems while providing full safety (within technological limits of course). This could allow us to fully wean off "web apps" and "apps" in general since they would be a new hybrid technology that isn't simply delivered by the web or installed per application. It's sort of like a modified and more capable version of X Windows. It could be a game changer if we can actually agree to merge open source with central planning and control.

Eventually everything gets replaced when something better comes along.

Somewhat like @Morbo hit on, the only reason our current set of webtools persists is inertia. Our current system of HTML+scripts is grossly outdated. The stateless human-readable source formatted text paradigm of HTML is far more of a hindrance than convenience to just about everything today. Even the most trivial modern page is going to be loaded with add-on after add-on to effect the most basic functionality. There is zero reason we couldn't have, for instance, the web instead deliver a simplified and low level byte code language in a stateful system with native bottom-up support for permission/parallelism/etc. Suddenly you have a million times more flexibility, a million times greater security (getting rid of necessitated javascript will instantly improve security by several orders of magnitude), and a million times greater performance on top of it all. But right now html+scripts runs just about everything and moving away from that is really hard. Many of the biggest companies could help effect such change, like Google, have also invested very heavily in the current system.

There have been a lot of attempts to do something like this such as with Java Applets, but these ideas have all been tie-ins instead of replacements and they all also suffer from lack of support. Something like this can't happen unless the major players all agree to it and get to partake in the creation of it.
